guidance: A reference for the IBM 029 card code and the 80-column card layout: it draws the holes for typed text and reads a column back. Card codes varied between keypunches and computer character sets, and a scanned card can be misread, so check a punch pattern against the equipment or the archival record you are working from before relying on it.
method: The IBM 029 keypunch divides each of the 80 card columns into 12 punch positions: the zone rows 12, 11 and 0, and the digit rows 1 to 9. A letter is one zone punch plus one digit punch, so A to I are 12-1 to 12-9, J to R are 11-1 to 11-9 and S to Z are 0-2 to 0-9; a digit is a single digit hole, with zero punched in row 0 alone; and a symbol adds a row 8 punch between the zone punch and the digit, so 8-2 is a colon, 12-8-3 is a period and 0-8-3 is a comma. Space is a column with no holes, and 0-8-2 is a non-printing blank that the keypunch uses to clear a column. That makes 64 codes in all, and the page lists every one with its 12-row punch pattern. Text is raised to capitals before punching, because the 029 set has no lowercase; a new line starts a new card and a card holds 80 columns, so up to eight cards (640 columns) are drawn at once. The column reader parses the rows in any order and returns the character, so 8-3-12 and 12-8-3 both read as a period. The character-to-punch table was transcribed from Doug Jones's 029 table and checked against the PDP-8 card reader table, which uses the same 12/11/0 zone and 1-9 digit assignments but prints a few of the multi-punch symbols differently: the 029 set gives the cent sign and the not sign to 12-8-2 and 11-8-7 where other machines print brackets or a caret. Everything is computed in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.
